quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.textToSpeak: The total came to fifty pounds.
quests.hint: Both fit a price. Listen for where the strongest beat falls.
quests.explanation: You heard "fifty": the beat landed on the first syllable and the ending was weak. In "fifteen" the last syllable is long and stressed.
quests.vowelTensionRule: The -teen numbers carry stress on the last syllable (/tiːn/) with a long vowel; the -ty numbers stress the first syllable and end in a weak /ti/. Listen for where the beat falls.
quests.mouthPosition: Stress the second syllable for -teen and lengthen the vowel. Stress the first syllable for -ty and shorten the second.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Either word works in this phrase. Listen to how wide the mouth opens at the start of the vowel.
quests.explanation: The word was "lane": it began at half-open and glided a short way. "Line" starts with a wider mouth.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Both are diphthongs that end in the same place, so listen to the beginning: open and low (/aɪ/) or mid (/eɪ/).
quests.mouthPosition: The glide is longer in /aɪ/ because the jaw starts lower.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Focus on the ending. Does it begin with a stop, or a smooth hush?
quests.explanation: That was "cash", ending with a smooth hush and no stop. "Catch" ends with a stop and then a hush.
quests.vowelTensionRule: /tʃ/ = /t/ + /ʃ/ in one movement; /ʃ/ has no stop.
quests.mouthPosition: Feel the tongue seal against the ridge before release for /tʃ/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Listen to how long the vowel is between the /sl/ and the /p/.
quests.explanation: "Sleep" holds a tense, long vowel before the lips close. "Slip" is quick and loose.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Both vowels are front and high, but /ɪ/ sits slightly lower and more relaxed. The sound your ear catches first is the difference in length: /iː/ lasts noticeably longer.
quests.mouthPosition: Try saying /iː/ with a wide, tense smile, then relax the cheeks and shorten the sound; that slack, quick version is /ɪ/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Both nouns fit. Is the vowel a little open, or tight?
quests.explanation: In the sentence, you caught "desk": the jaw was half open on the vowel. "Disk" is tighter and thinner.
quests.vowelTensionRule: /e/ sounds fuller and clearer, /ɪ/ sounds thinner and softer.
quests.mouthPosition: Keep the tongue tip near the lower front teeth in both; only the height of the tongue body changes.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Second sound of the word: a nasal hum, or a burst from the lips?
quests.explanation: The word was "smell": after the /s/, the lips closed for a hum. "Spell" pops the lips open instead.
quests.vowelTensionRule: A nasal consonant lets voiced air escape through the nose, while its oral partner blocks the nose and releases air from the mouth. Listen for a hum versus a burst.
quests.mouthPosition: For the nasal keep the nose open and hum; for the stop close off the nose and release air from the mouth. The lips or tongue tip make the same closure for both.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: The phrase suits both. Listen for a deep, rounded vowel or a thin, bright one.
quests.explanation: "Clock" has rounded lips and an open, deep vowel. "Click" is tight and bright.
quests.vowelTensionRule: The tongue travels from high-front to low-back between these two, so the vowel colour changes clearly.
quests.mouthPosition: Feel the tongue retreat and the lips round as you move to /ɒ/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Listen to how the vowel begins: neutral, or already rounded?
quests.explanation: It was "cold": the vowel began relaxed and closed into a round. "Called" holds a rounded shape steadily.
quests.vowelTensionRule: /əʊ/ has a starting point that is more central and an 'oo' ending; /ɔː/ has neither.
quests.mouthPosition: The jaw is more open for /ɔː/; for /əʊ/ it closes a little during the sound.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.textToSpeak: I left it on the coach.
quests.hint: The vowels match. Listen to the very end.
quests.explanation: "Coach" ends with a hush after the /t/. "Coat" stops at the /t/.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Listen for the hushing sound after the burst: it is there for /tʃ/ but not for /t/.
quests.mouthPosition: Add a small 'sh' after /t/ to create /tʃ/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Listen to the start of the word: one of them has an extra curl of the tongue.
quests.explanation: What you caught was "bread": the /b/ was followed by a curled /r/ before the vowel. "Bed" goes straight from the lips to the vowel.
quests.vowelTensionRule: One word has an extra /r/ right after the first consonant. That /r/ makes the beginning of the word sound curled and slightly longer, and the first stop loses some of its crispness.
quests.mouthPosition: After the first consonant, curl the tongue tip back for /r/ before the vowel. Without it, the consonant moves straight into the vowel.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Short, flat vowel or long, rounded one?
quests.explanation: "Lunch" is short, with relaxed lips. "Launch" is longer and needs rounded lips.
quests.vowelTensionRule: /ʌ/ is short, central and made with neutral lips; /ɔː/ is long, back and made with clearly rounded lips. Both length and lip shape help you tell them apart.
quests.mouthPosition: For /ʌ/ keep the lips relaxed and the jaw barely open. For /ɔː/ round the lips into a circle, pull the tongue back and hold the vowel longer.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.textToSpeak: I saw it start to bleed.
quests.hint: The consonant after the /b/ decides it. Contact or curl?
quests.explanation: You heard "bleed": the tongue tip touched the ridge after the /b/. In "breed" it would curl back.
quests.vowelTensionRule: After /k/, /ɡ/, /p/, /b/ or /f/, the /r/ pulls the lips and tongue back, while /l/ keeps the tongue tip forward.
quests.mouthPosition: Keep the lips slightly rounded through the cluster for /r/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.textToSpeak: It's nearly the end of term.
quests.hint: Both end with a hum. Do the lips close?
quests.explanation: The word was "term": the lips closed at the end. "Turn" finishes with the tongue tip against the ridge.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Listen to the nasal tail: rounded and lip-closing for /m/, bright and tongue-based for /n/.
quests.mouthPosition: Check that your lips touch for /m/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.textToSpeak: Take a look at the mouse.
quests.hint: Listen for a sharp hiss or a soft, airy ending.
quests.explanation: The word was "mouse": a sharp hiss with the tongue behind the teeth. "Mouth" ends with soft friction between the teeth.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Both are voiceless fricatives. The place of the tongue changes the quality of the hiss.
quests.mouthPosition: Keep the air flow gentle for /θ/ and focused for /s/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Something curls after the first stop in one of these. Which?
quests.explanation: "Trip" adds a curled /r/ after the /t/, so the start sounds like "chr". "Tip" flows directly into the vowel.
quests.vowelTensionRule: One word has an extra /r/ right after the first consonant. That /r/ makes the beginning of the word sound curled and slightly longer, and the first stop loses some of its crispness.
quests.mouthPosition: After the first consonant, curl the tongue tip back for /r/ before the vowel. Without it, the consonant moves straight into the vowel.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Same ending. Does the first sound begin with a stop?
quests.explanation: It was "sherry", which begins with a smooth hush. "Cherry" starts with a stop that releases into the hush.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Both are voiceless; the stop part is the clue.
quests.mouthPosition: Keep the lips slightly rounded for both.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: How wide does the mouth open as the vowel begins?
quests.explanation: "Light" opens wide at the start and closes. "Late" begins half open and travels a shorter distance.
quests.vowelTensionRule: /aɪ/ sounds like it begins with a bigger mouth opening.
quests.mouthPosition: Watch the jaw: a big movement for /aɪ/, a smaller one for /eɪ/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: One vowel moves, one stays steady. Which does this word have?
quests.explanation: What you caught was "loan": the vowel started relaxed and rounded off. "Lawn" is steady and rounded throughout.
quests.vowelTensionRule: /ɔː/ is a long, steady rounded vowel; /əʊ/ begins unrounded in the centre and glides to /ʊ/. Steady and rounded from the start versus a moving sound that rounds late.
quests.mouthPosition: For /ɔː/ round the lips from the start and keep them there. For /əʊ/ begin with relaxed lips and gradually round them.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: The vowel is either dull and short, or bright and wide.
quests.explanation: "Rush" is short and dull, with a nearly relaxed jaw. "Rash" is bright and wide.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Think 'wide and bright' for /æ/ against 'short and dull' for /ʌ/.
quests.mouthPosition: A big, wide mouth makes /æ/; a small, lazy mouth makes /ʌ/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Sharp hiss or broad hush at the start?
quests.explanation: That was "save": a thin, high hiss with spread lips. "Shave" begins with a broader hush and rounded lips.
quests.vowelTensionRule: The lips and tongue position both differ, and together they change the colour of the noise.
quests.mouthPosition: Watch your lips: they push forward for /ʃ/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Decide how long the vowel is, and whether the lips end up fully rounded.
quests.explanation: The word was "sport": a long vowel with tightly rounded lips. "Spot" is short and open.
quests.vowelTensionRule: In British English /ɔː/ is noticeably longer and 'darker' than /ɒ/, and it uses tighter lip rounding. /ɒ/ is short and more open.
quests.mouthPosition: Say /ɒ/ with a dropped jaw and a short beat; say /ɔː/ with rounder lips and a longer, steady vowel.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Both vowels are long. Are the lips rounded?
quests.explanation: You heard "walk": rounded lips and a darker vowel. "Work" is unrounded and more neutral.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Both vowels are long, so length will not help. Listen for lip rounding: none for /ɜː/, obvious for /ɔː/.
quests.mouthPosition: Say /ɜː/ with a lazy, flat mouth; for /ɔː/ purse the lips like blowing out a small flame.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Focus on the first sound. Is there a tongue closure, or only breath?
quests.explanation: "Jam" begins with a buzzing closure released into a hush. "Ham" begins with a puff of breath.
quests.vowelTensionRule: /dʒ/ begins with a complete closure of the tongue against the ridge and ends in hushing friction, and it is voiced; /h/ is only a breath from the throat, with no tongue closure at all.
quests.mouthPosition: For /dʒ/ press the tongue against the ridge behind the teeth, release into a hush and keep the voice on. For /h/ leave the tongue at rest and simply breathe out.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Same start and end. Is the vowel long and tense, or short and loose?
quests.explanation: It was "rich": a short, relaxed vowel before the /tʃ/. "Reach" stretches a high, tense vowel.
quests.vowelTensionRule: /iː/ is long and tense with the tongue high and forward; /ɪ/ is short, loose and a little lower and more central. Length and tension travel together, so a stretched vowel usually means /iː/.
quests.mouthPosition: For /iː/ spread the lips as if smiling and lift the tongue high behind the lower teeth. For /ɪ/ let the lips relax and drop the tongue a touch.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Both fit here. Is the vowel short and dull, or long and open?
quests.explanation: In this phrase, "staff" opened wide and stayed long. "Stuff" is short and relaxed.
quests.vowelTensionRule: /ɑː/ is the longer, deeper vowel with a wide-open mouth; /ʌ/ is a quick, relaxed sound from the middle of the mouth.
quests.mouthPosition: Open wide and hold it for /ɑː/; for /ʌ/ the jaw is barely open and the sound stops almost as soon as it starts.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Listen for a hushing sound after the first stop.
quests.explanation: What you caught was "test": a clean /t/ straight into the vowel. "Chest" adds a hush after the stop.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Both begin with the same closure; /tʃ/ adds friction.
quests.mouthPosition: Round the lips slightly for /tʃ/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Same ending. Front of the tongue or back for the first sound?
quests.explanation: "Table" starts with the tongue tip against the ridge. "Cable" starts with the back of the tongue lifting.
quests.vowelTensionRule: The alveolar stop is made with the tongue tip at the ridge behind the upper teeth; the velar stop is made with the back of the tongue at the soft palate. The velar release sounds deeper and more hollow.
quests.mouthPosition: For the alveolar stop touch the tongue tip to the ridge. For the velar stop lift the back of the tongue against the soft palate.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Listen to the consonant right after the /f/.
quests.explanation: That was "fruit": the tongue curled back after the /f/. "Flute" touches the ridge instead.
quests.vowelTensionRule: The tongue tip is forward and touching for /l/ and pulled back for /r/, even when it follows another consonant.
quests.mouthPosition: Feel the tongue tip move to the ridge for /l/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: The two words begin differently in the tongue. Is there any touching at the ridge?
quests.explanation: This time, you heard "road", with a curled tongue that never touches. "Load" taps the ridge behind the teeth.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Contact versus no contact: /l/ touches the ridge; /r/ hovers below it.
quests.mouthPosition: If your tongue touches the roof, you are making /l/; if it doesn't, /r/.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: The vowel is a slide in both. Listen to the hum at the end.
quests.explanation: The word was "foam": the lips closed at the end. "Phone" ends with the tongue tip on the ridge.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Both are voiced nasals; place of closure is the distinction.
quests.mouthPosition: Keep the lips relaxed for /n/.
